description: Proving when the planet is really changing. Is a hot summer or dry year just natural variation? For each place, Cassandra Signal builds 1,000 imaginary histories with the same natural ups and downs but no real trend. If the actual record stands apart from all 1,000, natural variation has no alibi. It also backtests past droughts and issues locked-in seasonal forecasts scored after the season. One shareable card per place. NASA POWER + GISTEMP v4. Python, static site, GitHub Pages.
summary: Cassandra Signal proves when a place's climate is really changing. Every hot summer or dry year raises the same question: is this just natural variation? For each location, Cassandra Signal builds 1,000 imaginary climate histories from NASA POWER data that share the place's real natural ups and downs and year-to-year memory, but contain no long-term trend. If the real record stands apart from all 1,000, natural variation has no alibi. Our first eight places show it clearly: São Paulo, London, Sydney and Nairobi are warming faster than all 1,000 histories allow. To earn trust, it backtests past droughts using only data that existed at the time, and it locks in seasonal forecasts with a public fingerprint before each season, then scores them afterwards, misses included. Each place gets one shareable card: a plain-language verdict, the evidence and the track record. Built with NASA POWER and NASA GISTEMP v4, in Python, as a free static site on GitHub Pages.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Cassandra Signal answers one question for any place on Earth: is the climate here really changing, or is this within normal natural variation? For each place it gives a plain-language verdict for temperature and for rainfall, the evidence behind it, and its own public track record.

HOW IT WORKS

1. NASA data: monthly 2 m air temperature (T2M) and bias-corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR) for each place from the NASA POWER API, 1981 to the latest month, with NASA GISTEMP v4 global anomalies for context (the planet has warmed 0.21 °C per decade since 1981).

2. Remove the seasons: each month is compared with its own 1981-2010 normal, then averaged per year. Rainfall becomes a percent of normal.

3. Learn natural variation: after removing any trend, we measure how big the natural swings are and how much one year carries into the next (an AR(1) model).

4. 1,000 imaginary histories: we generate 1,000 records with exactly that natural behaviour and no trend, and measure each one's trend with Sen's slope, a robust method that one wild year cannot fool.

5. The verdict: if the real trend is more extreme than all 1,000, natural variation alone has less than a 1-in-1,000 chance of explaining it ("Natural variation has no alibi"). Weaker evidence gives "Very unlikely natural", "Probably real" or "Not yet". A second, independent kind of imaginary history (IAAFT surrogates) double-checks every verdict.

6. Backtests: we stand in the year before a documented drought, use only data that existed then, and ask how rare the drought's driest year was. Fresno's 2013 had 24% of normal rain (drier than 98% of natural years), São Paulo's 2014 53%, Sydney's 2019 51%, Nairobi's 2022 53%. Before the 2017-2019 drought, Sydney's warming was already "very unlikely natural". Cape Town is a miss: its NASA POWER grid cell is partly ocean and did not capture its mountain-catchment drought.

7. Locked-in forecasts: before each December-February season, a forecast (chance of cooler, near or warmer than normal) is saved with a SHA-256 fingerprint and committed publicly, so it cannot be changed later. It is scored after the season with the Ranked Probability Score against simply guessing 33/33/33. Ten-year hindcasts show the track record, including places where the simple method does worse than guessing.

8. Output: one shareable 1200x630 card per place plus a page with full charts, the backtest, the forecast and the data.

FIRST RESULTS (1981-2025)

Temperature: "Natural variation has no alibi" in São Paulo (+0.39 °C per decade), London (+0.39), Sydney (+0.31) and Nairobi (+0.26). "Very unlikely natural" in Fresno (+0.35) and Mumbai (+0.13). "Not yet" in Latur and Cape Town. Rainfall: São Paulo drying (-9.7% of normal per decade, no alibi), Mumbai wetting (+11.7%), most others "Not yet".

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It gives communities, farmers, students, journalists and local decision makers a fair, testable answer instead of opinion. It can say "not yet", it shows its misses, and it publishes forecasts before the results are known, so anyone can check its record. Every card is free to share and every step is open source and reproducible.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, Matplotlib, requests), pytest (12 tests), the NASA POWER API, NASA GISTEMP v4, HTML/CSS, Git and GitHub, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for free static hosting. The 28.6-second demo video is rendered by our own Python script from the real website and NASA-data charts (ffmpeg via imageio-ffmpeg), with subtitles and an AI-generated narration voice (ElevenLabs via Higgsfield), labelled on screen.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Rather than a single warming line, it puts each place's climate record on trial against 1,000 alternative histories, and it keeps a fingerprinted, public track record of its own predictions. The name comes from Cassandra, whose true warnings nobody believed: we make warnings believable.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Natural year-to-year memory (a dry year makes the next more likely). Short records, which make trend tests cry wolf: we correct for this and tested the method on 400 made-up trend-free records, where it raised false alarms only 2.8% to 5.0% of the time (a fair test is about 5%). Never using future data in backtests. Grid-cell data versus local stations. Plain language for non-experts. Showing failures as clearly as successes. Free, open and reproducible tools.
